title: Solving the equation of value for an unknown time or interest rate
status: reviewed and locally validated; passes 1-9 complete; gate 6b passed round 3 (0 blocking)

Instructor: the title slides of Lectures 12 and 13 (f0001 of each, viewed at full size) name Prof. Neelesh S. Upadhye, IIT Madras; the slide footers repeat the name. No other presenter is named in the frames viewed.

Reference-mapping boxes on the roadmap slides (slide facts, not cited, books not open): Lecture 12 (f0005) Broverman section 2.2.4, Chan and Tse section 1.8; Lecture 13 (f0004) Broverman sections 2.2.5 and 2.4.1, Chan and Tse section 4.1.

Lecture 12 f0048 prints Balance_6 = 5000(1.4185) - 1000(6.9753) = 7092.50 - 6975.30 = 117.20 and a drop payment 117.20 x 1.06 = 124.23. With unrounded factors the balance is 117.28 and the drop payment 124.31 (rounding 1.418519 to 1.4185 removes 0.10 from the loan term; rounding 6.975319 to 6.9753 removes 0.02 from the payment term). The chapter gives both and uses the exact values.

Lecture 13 f0014 prints v = 0.931 and i = (1/v) - 1 = 7.41%. The positive root of 5v^2 + 5v - 9 = 0 is 0.931782, so i = 7.3212%; 7.41% (7.4114%) is the result of inverting the rounded v. The chapter reports both and uses the case as an instance of the rounding rule.

Lecture 13 f0032 and f0035 report the calculator IRR as 13.06%. The exact root of 100 = 60v + 60v^2 is 13.0662%, which rounds to 13.07% at two decimals; 13.06% is the root truncated. The calculator display was not reproduced; the chapter reports the slide's 13.06% and the exact 13.0662%.

Lecture 13 f0028 prints 60(1.1)^-1 = 54.54 (60/1.1 = 54.545) and f0041 prints 191.66 and 91.66 at 20% (230/1.2 = 191.667, 132/1.44 = 91.667); the sums and conclusions are unaffected. The chapter notes the printed values.

Lecture 12 f0055 writes the number of quarters as m in (1.02)^m = 2; the chapter writes N because m is the conversion frequency of i^(m) (chapter 2). The slide's i^(4) in the problem line is partly hidden at the slide edge; the speech and the computation 8%/4 = 2% confirm a nominal 8% convertible quarterly.

Lecture 12 f0033 is titled 'The Balloon Payment Scenario' although the slide that follows (f0037) defines option B as the balloon and the lecture works only option A, the drop payment. The chapter treats both conventions and computes the balloon payment (1,117.28) itself.
Lecture 12 f0020: the rule of 72 is described as highly accurate for 2%-10% with errors growing above 20%. The chapter quantifies this (Table 5.1) and does not repeat 'highly accurate' as a finding.

Lecture 13 f0044 (summary): 'Algebra: works only for single payments or quadratics (n = 2)' and 'Uniqueness: guaranteed only if cash flow signs change once'. The chapter attributes the first as a statement about hand methods and does not rely on it. On the second: one sign change guarantees uniqueness (proved in the chapter); 'only if' is not proved and is not repeated, since a stream with two sign changes can also have exactly one rate (the double root at c = 132.25, Exercise 4).

Lecture 13 calls linear interpolation 'the exam method' and calculator iteration 'the practitioner's method'; these are the speaker's descriptions. The chapter attributes them and cites SOA syllabus p. 1 on calculators and approximation methods.
Descartes' rule of signs is quoted from the slide (f0038) and attributed; no open source for it is cited and the chapter does not prove it. The chapter proves the one-sign-change case directly.

TI guidebook p. 41 (PDF p. 46) states that with two or more sign changes at least one IRR solution exists. The stream -100, +230, -140 (discriminant -3,100) has two sign changes and no real rate; the chapter states that the guidebook's sentence does not hold for this stream and gives a correct sufficient condition with proof. The guidebook is cited only for what the calculator does.

Caption errors corrected from the slides (paraphrased): in Lecture 12 the geometric-series sum is spoken with plus signs where the slide (f0030) has a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r); the drop payment 'at time 0.7' is t = 7 on the slide (f0048); in Lecture 13 the result of 1.5^(1/5) is spoken as 0.2 where the slide (f0007) has i = (1.5)^0.2 - 1; c is spoken once as 9 where the slide (f0011) has -9; the interpolated rate is spoken as 13.3 where the slide (f0031, f0032) has 13.13%; one spoken value 104.3 is 104.13 on the slide.
Equated time (section 'Several payments replaced by one') is not covered by Lectures 12 or 13; it is an original extension, labelled as such on the page, with its own proof.
Shared CSS: assets/book.css has no rule for the classes lead and source-note (as recorded by chapter 7); the chapter uses them as the brief requires. Not edited (shared file).

sections.section: The running case and the tools from earlier in the course
sections.lecture_material: The equation of value as the tool for cash flows moved to a focal date; FV = PV(1+i)^n under compounding; the questions of an unknown i and an unknown n.
sections.teaching_construction: Restatement, taken as given from earlier in the course, of the effective rate and compound accumulation (5.1), v and 1 - v = iv (5.2), the equation of value and the independence of the focal date under one rate, the geometric series (5.3) with c and q instead of the slide's a and r, and logarithms; the rounding rule; the running case (loan of 20,000 with offers A, B, C, invented terms); the formal model.

sections.section: Unknown time for a single sum: logarithms and doubling
sections.lecture_material: Isolate n: (1+i)^n = FV/PV, take natural logs, n = ln(FV/PV)/ln(1+i) (f0010); exponential growth meeting a target line, n on the x-axis (f0013); doubling at 6%: ln2/ln1.06 = 0.6931/0.05827, n = 11.896 years (f0016); amount invested does not matter.
sections.teaching_construction: Uniqueness from monotonicity; sign of n for FV < PV; units of n; why a fractional time needs no interpretation for a single sum; substitution check and the limit i -> 0.

sections.section: The rule of 72 as an approximation to the exact time
sections.lecture_material: Rule of 72, n = 72/(100 i), 72/6 = 12 years; approximation warning: accurate for 2%-10%, error margin increases above about 20% (f0020).
sections.teaching_construction: Series derivation (5.5), n = ln2 (1/i + 1/2 - i/12 + ...); why 72 suits rates near 8%; proof that ln(1+i)/i decreases, so the rule is exact at exactly one rate, 7.8469%, overestimating below and underestimating above; Table 5.1 of errors at 2%, 6%, 8%, 10%, 20%, 50%.

sections.section: The present value of a level stream of payments
sections.lecture_material: Loan of 5000 as the PV of future payments; PV = 1000v + 1000v^2 + ... + 1000v^n; geometric progression with a = 1000v, r = v; PV = 1000v(1 - v^n)/(1 - v); 1 - v = iv gives PV = 1000(1 - v^n)/i (f0030); terminology deferred to the annuity week.
sections.teaching_construction: General payment R; symbol a angle n as an abbreviation of the bracket; limit i -> 0 and bounds a < n, a < 1/i; the running case values 2500 a angle 12 = 19,856.72 and 2500 a angle 13 = 20,894.13 at 7%.
General formula (5.7) with the existence condition R > Li and its meaning; running case A: n = 12.1342; floor(n) payments too few, floor(n)+1 too many, with values.

sections.section: Non-integer terms: the drop payment and the balloon payment
sections.lecture_material: Interpreting n = 6.12: option A drop payment (6 full payments, smaller 7th at t = 7), option B balloon payment (5 full payments, larger 6th at t = 6), focus on option A (f0037); accumulating the payments, FV = 1000[(1+i)^k - 1]/i, notation s angle k (f0043); Balance_6 = 5000(1.06)^6 - 1000 s angle 6 = 7092.50 - 6975.30 = 117.20, drop 124.23 (f0048); general strategy Drop = (L(1+i)^k - R s angle k)(1+i) (f0051); summary (f0057).
sections.research_extension: SOA Exam FM syllabus p. 3, topic 3a: final payment (drop payment, balloon payment).
sections.teaching_construction: Balance (5.9), drop (5.10), balloon (5.11); exact values 117.28, 124.31, 1,117.28 and the source of the slide's 8-cent difference; check of both schedules by the equation of value at t = 0; proof that 0 < drop < R; fractional part 121.19 against 124.31; running case A: B12 = 322.70, drop 345.29 at t = 13, balloon 2,822.70 at t = 12 after 11 full payments (check 18,746.69 + 1,253.31 = 20,000.00), fractional part 335.39 (9.90 short), total 30,345.29 (drop) and 30,322.70 (balloon).

sections.lecture_material: Doubling at i(4) = 8%: quarterly rate 2%, (1.02)^m = 2, m = ln2/ln1.02 = 35.003 quarters, 8.75 years (f0055).
sections.research_extension: None (chapter 2, committed, is referred to for the definition of i(m)).
sections.teaching_construction: N in place of the slide's m; the same answer through the effective annual rate 8.2432%; the error of using ln 1.08 (9.0065 years, 0.2558 too long).

sections.section: Several payments replaced by one: equated time and exact time
sections.teaching_construction: Exact single-payment time by (5.4); equated time (5.12); proof by the tangent-line inequality for the convex v^x that the equated time is later than the exact time for i > 0; example 10,000 at t = 2 and 20,000 at t = 8 at 6%: 6 against 5.7588, loss of 299.40 in present value; 5.9599 at 1%; expansion t = t-bar - (1/2) ln(1+i) sigma^2 + O(ln(1+i)^2) with sigma^2 the amount-weighted variance of the dates (t-bar is the limit as i -> 0; the gap is first order), checked: 0.2331 against 0.2412 at 6%, 0.0398 against 0.0401 at 1%.

sections.section: Why an unknown rate is harder: the single sum
sections.lecture_material: Roadmap: analytic method, linear interpolation (the exam method), calculator iteration (the practitioner's method) (f0004); case 1: 100(1+i)^5 = 150, i = 1.5^0.2 - 1; case 2: 100 = 10v + 20v^2 + 100v^3, hard (f0007); summary: algebra works only for single payments or quadratics (f0044).
sections.teaching_construction: Formula (5.13) with uniqueness; i = 8.4472%; running case C: 1.85^0.1 - 1 = 6.3450%; the summary claim attributed as a statement about hand methods; lender B's equation of degree 10.

sections.section: Two payments: a quadratic in the discount factor
sections.teaching_construction: Exact root 0.931782 and i = 7.3212%; the slide's 7.41% traced to rounding v (sensitivity di/dv = -1/v^2); substitution check 179.78 against 180.00; when two payments give a quadratic; uniqueness from the product of the roots -L/c2 < 0.

sections.section: Linear interpolation and the convexity gap
sections.lecture_material: Guess a low rate (PV above target) and a high rate (PV below target), assume a straight line (f0020); interpolation formula i = i_L + (PV_L - Target)/(PV_L - PV_H)(i_H - i_L) by similar triangles; pick i_L and i_H close together (f0024); example 100 = 60v + 60v^2: 104.13 at 10%, 97.54 at 15% (f0028), 13.13% (f0031); convexity gap: convex PV curve, line above the curve, interpolated rate too high; calculator 13.06% (f0032).
sections.teaching_construction: Exact root 13.0662% from the quadratic 6v^2 + 6v - 10 = 0; proof (5.16) that PV is decreasing and convex for positive payments and that the interpolated rate is never below the root; Figure 5.1 with the wide bracket 2%-40% (16.57% against 13.07%); error formula PV''(i0)(i0 - iL)(iH - i0)/(2|PV'(i0)|) with the check 0.000692 against 0.000691; bracket table (0.0691, 0.0116, 0.000722, 0.0000261 points); running case B: 20,608.24 at 6%, 19,666.03 at 7%, interpolation 6.6455% against 6.6373%.

sections.lecture_material: BA II Plus IRR: CF key, CF0 = -100, C01 = 60, F01 = 2, IRR then CPT, result 13.06% (f0035); the speech describes the calculator result as the exact answer.
sections.research_extension: TI BA II PLUS guidebook p. 40: IRR is the rate at which NPV = 0, computed by iterative calculations. SOA Exam FM syllabus p. 1: calculators remove the need to learn certain methods of approximation.
sections.teaching_construction: Net present value f and the bracket condition; bisection with the stopping rule hi - lo <= tolerance, 40 halvings from [1e-9, 1] at 1e-12, roots 13.0662% and 6.6373%, substitution check (5e-11 and -3e-8 dollars) and its scale (|f'| about 93,000, midpoint error <= 5e-13); false position as repeated interpolation, with a proof of convergence under (5.16) (monotone high ends, limit is the root), stopping rule |f| < 1e-9 and mean-value-theorem upper bound |x - i0| <= |f(x)|/|f'(x)| (|f'| decreases with the rate), giving errors below 1e-11 and 1e-13 at the respective stopping points; errors falling by a factor of about 28 per step, 7 and 8 steps.

sections.section: Several sign changes: uniqueness and multiple rates
sections.lecture_material: Descartes' rule of signs: positive real roots at most the number of sign changes; normal loan -100, +50, +50, +50, unique i; complex project -100, +230, -132, potential for two roots (f0038); mine closure -100 + 230v - 132v^2 = 0 satisfied at 10% and 20% (f0039, f0041); summary: uniqueness only with one sign change (f0044).
sections.research_extension: TI BA II PLUS guidebook pp. 40-41 (number of IRR solutions and sign changes; display of the solution closest to zero; Error 7) and pp. 79-80 (Error 5, Error 7).
sections.teaching_construction: Proof (5.17) of at most one rate for one sign change; existence from the signs of the first and last coefficients; positivity iff undiscounted sum > 0; exact factorization of the mine closure; NPV -2 at 0%, 0.19 at 15%; the stream with cleanup 140 and no rate (discriminant -3,100, NPV at most -5.5357); the guidebook's 'at least one solution' sentence contradicted, with a correct sufficient condition.

Table 5.2 (terms, rates, totals, PV at an invented 5%); uniqueness and positivity of each rate; rankings by rate, by total and by present value; crossing rates 5.4313% (C = A) and 6.0540% (C = B); the decision rule and the general procedure.

sections.section: Executable check of the methods and the running case
sections.teaching_construction: Standard-library program: (5.4), (5.6), (5.7), (5.8), (5.10), (5.11), (5.15), bisection, false position, sign count; assertions that both final-payment schedules satisfy the equation of value; ValueError cases; grid illustration of the largest NPV; two fault injections described (drop without interest: AssertionError; wrong numerator in (5.15): ValueError after 100 steps).

sections.section: What these methods establish and what they do not
sections.research_extension: SOA Exam FM syllabus p. 2 (outcomes 1b, 1d) and p. 3 (topic 3).
sections.teaching_construction: Exact results, approximations with error sign, and iterations with guarantees; definitions, model and convention; where the methods stop applying (non-integer terms, several sign changes, changing rates, simple interest).

sections.lecture_material: Exercises 1 and 2 extend the drop-payment example of Lecture 12; Exercise 4 extends the mine closure of Lecture 13; Exercise 5 tests the Lecture 13 summary on interpolation.
sections.teaching_construction: Six original exercises with full solutions: derive (5.7), the final-payment identities and the bounds; exam-style closest-of-five drop payment with each distractor tied to an error; check an assumption (rule of 72 at a monthly, nominal and effective rate); counterexample (two sign changes and no rate; double root at c = 132.25; the guidebook sentence); counterexample to the interpolation summary (accumulated-value form underestimates, 7.2739% against 7.2792%); equated time against exact time with a judgment (6.1 against 5.4992, 591.86; gap predicted by the expansion 0.6038 against 0.6008, variance 15.69).

references.title: Lecture 12 recording, Solving for Unknown Time (n)
references.supports: Logarithm solution for n, doubling time, rule of 72, sum of a level stream, loan of 5,000 and n = 6.12, drop and balloon options, s angle k, balance and drop payment, general strategy, doubling at 8% convertible quarterly.

references.title: Lecture 13 recording, Solving for Unknown Interest Rate (i)
references.supports: Single-sum rate, cubic example, quadratic in v, linear interpolation and its formula, convexity gap, IRR keystrokes, Descartes' rule of signs as stated, mine closure.

references.title: Texas Instruments, BA II PLUS Calculator guidebook (English)
references.supports: p. 40: IRR is the interest rate at which the net present value of the cash flows is equal to 0; the calculator performs a series of iterative calculations; the number of possible IRR solutions depends on the number of sign changes; no sign change, no IRR solution (Error 5); one sign change, only one IRR solution. p. 41: with two or more sign changes, as many solutions can exist as there are sign changes (and the sentence 'at least one solution exists', which the chapter shows false for one stream); when more than one solution exists the calculator displays the one closest to zero, which has no financial meaning; the calculator might not find IRR even if a solution exists (Error 7). pp. 79-80: Error 5 (IRR computed without at least one sign change), Error 7 (iteration limit exceeded, complex problem with multiple sign changes).

references.title: Society of Actuaries, Financial Mathematics Exam -- October 2026 syllabus
references.supports: p. 1: candidates may use specified calculators, which eliminate the need to learn and be examined on certain mathematical methods of approximation. p. 2: outcome 1b, given any three of interest rate, period of time, present value and future value, calculate the remaining item; outcome 1d, write the equation of value given a set of cash flows and an interest rate. p. 3: topic 3a, final payment (drop payment, balloon payment); 3b, the missing item given four of term, rate, payment amount, payment period and principal.
